extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research integrity officers, and publication ethicists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for deciding authorship when an article is retracted for research misconduct and then revised and resubmitted (retract-and-replace/republication) — including policy review, ethical analysis, and case factors to weigh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research misconduct (US federal definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research misconduct means fabrication, falsification, or plagiarism in proposing, performing, or reviewing research, or in reporting research results. Research misconduct does not include honest error or differences of opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove misconduct under this policy, an institution or funding agency must find (a) a significant departure from accepted practices of the relevant research community and (b) that the misconduct was committed intentionally, knowingly or recklessly. The standard of proof is preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not). Note: other countries and institutions may adopt broader definitions (including improper authorship, undisclosed conflicts, confidentiality breaches, interference with investigations, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: ICMJE authorship criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICMJE recommends that authorship be based on the following four criteria: (1) Substantial contributions to the conception or design of the work; or the acquisition, analysis, or interpretation of data for the work; AND (2) Drafting the work or revising it critically for important intellectual content; AND (3) Final approval of the version to be published; AND (4) Agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work in ensuring that questions related to the accuracy or integrity of any part of the work are appropriately investigated and resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All those designated as authors should meet all four criteria, and all who meet the four criteria should be identified as authors. Those who do not meet all four criteria should be acknowledged. ICMJE also states that an author should be able to identify which co-authors are responsible for specific other parts of the work and have confidence in the integrity of co-authors' contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: COPE minimum authorship requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: COPE states that the minimum requirements for authorship, common to all definitions, are (1) substantial contribution to the work and (2) accountability for the work that was done and its presentation in a publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COPE defers to disciplinary organisations to provide detailed authorship criteria. COPE guidance therefore does not resolve nuanced questions (e.g., whether a person found guilty of misconduct should be an author on a resubmitted paper) because it leaves 'substantial' and 'accountability' underspecified and context-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant (substantial) contribution as an authorship standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship should be awarded only for significant contributions (e.g., conception/design, data acquisition, analysis, interpretation, development of methods or reagents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and guidelines list roles that commonly qualify as significant contributions but typically do not define precisely what counts as 'substantial' — this is a contextual, discipline-specific judgment. In the retract-and-republish context, a central evaluative question is whether the accused person’s contributions to the revised paper remain 'significant'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability requirement for authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: An author should be able to be accountable for all aspects of the work and identify which co-authors are responsible for specific parts of the work; authors should have confidence in the integrity of their co-authors' contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accountability is especially salient when misconduct has occurred: coauthors may question whether the person who committed misconduct can or will be accountable. This affects whether inclusion as an author is appropriate. ICMJE-level accountability can be undermined by refusing to permit approval of the final version as an anti-pattern for excluding someone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and transparency in authorship lists and contribution statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship lists and contribution statements must reflect the truth about who did the work; financial and other supports and contributors should be fully disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honorary authorship (credit where none is due) and ghost authorship (omitting those who contributed) are unethical. Transparency includes noting contributions and conflicts of interest so readers can evaluate credibility. In retract-and-replace cases, transparency may require linking to the retracted article and explaining corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: CRediT contributor-roles taxonomy as a clarifying tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRediT system distinguishes between 14 categories of contributor activities (e.g., data curation, formal analysis, methodology, supervision) to clarify who did what.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CRediT helps make contributions explicit and may be used in lieu of or alongside authorship to describe roles. However, CRediT does not itself define or replace authorship; it is a transparency tool that can help determine whether someone’s contributions merit authorship or acknowledgement in difficult cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case inclusion criteria for identifying retracted-and-republished examples
rubrics_metrics.description: A case met the study criteria if: (1) the article was retracted; (2) the stated reason for the retraction was research misconduct; and (3) the article was republished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors used searches of PubMed, Retraction Watch, and ORI databases and excluded items where retractions were for honest error or where corrections (not retractions) left the original article in place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal policy coding rule used in policy review
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal policy was coded as addressing the authorship/misconduct/retract-and-resubmit issue only if it specifically described or referred to that issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General authorship, retraction, correction, or misconduct policies that did not explicitly mention the specific scenario (misconduct-caused retraction followed by resubmission) were not counted as addressing the issue. Independent double-coding was used to ensure reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors supporting inclusion of a person who committed misconduct as an author
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments for including such a person: (a) fairness — credit should be given where due for significant contributions; (b) accountability — naming them allows them to help explain and defend parts of the work; (c) honesty/transparency — omitting them misrepresents who contributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These arguments assume the person’s contribution to the revised manuscript is still significant and that they can or will be accountable. Inclusion may also be less controversial when misconduct did not affect the salvaged data or when misconduct was less egregious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors supporting exclusion of a person who committed misconduct as an author
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments for excluding such a person: (a) fairness may require denying benefits to someone who violated ethical norms; (b) including them could morally taint the research and harm coauthors' reputations; (c) their ability to be accountable and trustworthy may be compromised; (d) sanctions (e.g., debarment, institutional requirements) may mandate removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions to exclude should consider the severity and mental state of the misconduct, the nature of the contribution used in the resubmitted paper, and any institutional or funder-imposed sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of mental state in adjudicating misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The mental state descriptors 'intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly' are important: intentionally = with meaning or purpose; knowingly = with full awareness; recklessly = careless or indifferent to the welfare of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The culpability of the respondent varies with mental state; intentionally or knowingly committed misconduct is more egregious than recklessness. Mental state affects moral blameworthiness and may influence whether the person should be listed as an author on a resubmitted paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction/correction/retract-and-replace distinction and transparency expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may retract, correct, or 'retract and replace' (retract and republish) depending on severity and whether salvageable material remains. Republishing often links to the original retracted article, which stays in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, retraction notices often use vague wording (e.g., 'data unreliable') and may avoid naming responsible parties to reduce libel risk. Best practices suggested by the discussion include clearly linking retracted and republished versions and explaining what was corrected and why to maintain transparency in the research record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of acknowledgements and detailed contribution statements as alternatives to authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: When including a person as an author is contested, their contributions may be described in acknowledgements and detailed contributor-role statements (e.g., CRediT) instead of authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledgement plus explicit description of contributions may satisfy some norms (honesty, transparency, partial accountability) without conferring authorship credit. However, this may be contested as insufficient by those who argue for credit where due.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition/anti-pattern: denying authorship by withholding approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who wish to exclude someone could refuse to allow them to read and approve the final version, thereby disqualifying them under ICMJE criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICMJE prohibits this manipulative tactic, but it still occurs. Such behaviour is an unethical method of excluding contributors and compromises fairness and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of institutions and research integrity officers (RIOs) in resolving authorship disputes after misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions and RIOs can be consulted to provide guidance when coauthors disagree about including an individual found to have committed misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolution should be case-by-case, consider institutional findings/sanctions, and may require coordination between authors, institutions, and journal editors to ensure integrity, appropriate credit, and compliance with sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical finding: top biomedical journals lacked specific guidance on misconduct→retract→resubmit authorship issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Review of authorship, retraction, correction, and misconduct policies from ICMJE, COPE, and fifteen top biomedical journals found that none specifically addressed authorship when a paper is retracted for misconduct and then republished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most top journals have authorship policies and many have retraction/correction/misconduct policies, but the absence of explicit guidance on this scenario suggests a policy gap and the need for journals/institutions to develop specific guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological criterion for coding journal policy presence
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing journals, the authors distinguished between a journal having its own policy and following COPE or ICMJE, and reviewed four types of policies: authorship, retraction, correction, and misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A policy was considered to 'address the issue' only if it specifically described or referred to authorship in cases of retraction due to misconduct followed by resubmission; general guidance did not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing norms framework for authorship decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship decisions should be assessed in light of four mutually reinforcing norms: fairness, accountability, honesty, and transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These norms can pull in different directions in retract-and-republish cases (e.g., fairness may favor crediting a contributor, but fairness may also require denying benefits to someone who committed misconduct). Decision-makers should articulate how each norm applies in the specific case and weigh them accordingly.
